source.title: Some Fundamental Aspects about Lipschitz Continuity of Neural Network Functions

page_placements.theme: Input sensitivity and decision-boundary fragmentation around interpolation

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling. The text identifies the paper as published at ICLR 2024, despite the supplied venue metadata.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps network width and reports test-loss curves around the interpolation threshold, alongside Lipschitz measurements. Its width-sweep/test-loss setup directly tests model-wise double descent, though much of the paper focuses on Lipschitz behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-loss curves in figures for width sweeps, and explicitly says the CIFAR-100 test-loss trend mirrors the Lipschitz double-descent trend. Other plotted test-loss curves are recorded as figure-only where the text does not describe their shape. Lipschitz trends are recorded separately under fits_no_version because they are not test error. Cited results from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study reruns a Nakkiran-style CNN width sweep on CIFAR-100, plus FCN, CNN and ViT sweeps in the appendix, and plots test loss around the interpolation threshold. The text states the test-loss trend has a double-descent shape for several sweeps. Its main focus is Lipschitz bounds, which belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors' main conclusions are about Lipschitz constants. The lower bound is faithful to the effective Lipschitz constant. Lipschitz grows substantially during training. Over-parameterisation implicitly regularises the Lipschitz constant, giving double-descent-like non-monotonicity in its bounds that mirrors test loss. Label noise, capacity and memorisation interact. Test-loss double descent is used as the setting rather than being the object of study.
record.recipe_differences: Uses width sweeps around the interpolation threshold and test-loss measurement, but focuses substantially on Lipschitz bounds and tests its own architecture and dataset settings rather than presenting an explicit replication of either original source.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes are examined across architecture, dataset, loss, and label-shuffling conditions. The text specifically reports that label noise shifts the Lipschitz memorisation threshold toward higher parameter counts.

fits_no_version.finding: All three Lipschitz bounds rise to the interpolation threshold and fall afterward with width (CIFAR-100 CNN and other settings).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lipschitz bounds show a double-descent-like trend with network width.

fits_no_version.finding: The lower Lipschitz bound is non-monotonic across width and label noise, and its memorisation threshold shifts to higher parameter counts with noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label noise shifts the Lipschitz memorisation threshold toward larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: The lower Lipschitz bound grows 63× and 40× from initialisation over training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lipschitz constants grow substantially over training even for very wide networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Lipschitz bounds rise sublinearly with training-set size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Function complexity, measured by the Lipschitz constant, increases with sample count.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameter distance travelled at the last epoch shows double descent with width (Fig S31).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter displacement from initialisation shows a double-descent trend across width.

record.problems: Several relevant test-loss outcomes are available only as figures without an explicit textual description or numerical values. The clear textual test-loss double-descent statement is for one CNN/CIFAR-100 setting. The sample-size and epoch-evolution evidence relevant to other claim versions measures Lipschitz bounds rather than test error.
record.rows_left_out: Other Lipschitz plots and auxiliary measurements in the appendices are not separately catalogued where they do not test the test-error versions, repeat a reported pattern without a distinct condition, or concern unrelated regularization/evaluation questions. The paper's values for test-loss curves are generally plotted rather than tabulated.

untested.parts: Epoch-wise test error is not reported; only Lipschitz evolution over training.
The sample-size experiment (S3.20) reports Lipschitz bounds only, not test error.
No non-neural model classes are tested, and the claim of subsuming the U-shaped curve is not tested.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location across axes.
Whether optimally tuned regularisation removes the peak is not tested. Label noise's effect on the test-loss peak is plotted but not described. Triple descent is only speculated.
No re-counting of effective parameters is done.

missing.what: Bias-variance decomposition of test loss: the double-descent shape is driven mostly by variance, with bias nearly constant across widths.
Remark that FCN MNIST1D test loss rises again after the second descent, possibly triple descent (speculative).
missing.locator: Appendix S3.9, remark on Figure S12

missing.what: Test loss on adversarially perturbed and OOD test samples across the width sweep (figure only).

record.verdict_notes: Test-loss evidence is mostly figure-only. The double-descent statements on test loss are brief and secondary to the Lipschitz analysis. V4 links were removed because all models are neural networks. The regularisation result uses a Lipschitz constraint that was not tuned, so it supports a reduced peak but not the version's claim that the peak disappears.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests width sweeps in its reported datasets and architectures, but does not establish that the pattern holds for all deep networks or settings.
Test error over training epochs is not tested; epoch-wise measurements concern Lipschitz bounds.
The number-of-training-samples experiment reports Lipschitz bounds, not whether increasing sample count raises test error near interpolation.
The study reports width-sweep test-loss plots for several neural-network architectures, but does not test non-neural model classes or establish a general account across model classes.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study varies label-shuffling level and capacity and plots test loss, but does not establish that noise or variance causes the peak, test triple or multiple descent as a test-error result, or test whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
The paper does not test whether counting effective parameters converts a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
